extraction.name: MATH Dataset
extraction.description: A dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems with full step-by-step solutions, designed to measure mathematical problem-solving ability in machine learning models. The paper also introduces AMPS, a large auxiliary mathematics pretraining corpus.
extraction.creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt
extraction.publisher: NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
extraction.citeAs: Hendrycks, D. et al. Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The MATH dataset was collected from mathematics competitions including AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and more, with many problems collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. AMPS was collected from Khan Academy exercises and Mathematica-generated problems using manually designed scripts.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Document analysis, Web Scraping, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Competition mathematics problems from the Mathematical Association of America (AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and more); Khan Academy exercises; Mathematica-generated problems from 100 manually designed scripts.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For AMPS, the authors generated approximately 5 million problems using Mathematica scripts, with around 50,000 exercises per script. They also upsampled Khan Academy data by a factor of 5 and downsampled Mathematica data by a factor of 2 during pretraining.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions were consistently formatted using LaTeX and Asymptote. Final boxed answers were normalized with formatting rules for exact-match evaluation, including fraction normalization, ignoring spaces, and treating equivalent expressions as the same.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each MATH problem has a full step-by-step solution and a final boxed answer. The paper states that problems are carefully curated by the competition mathematics community. For AMPS, 37 of the 100 Mathematica modules include full step-by-step LaTeX solutions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper notes that step-by-step solutions can be used as scratch space, but model-generated solutions may contain logical mistakes. Final answers are evaluated by parsing the content inside \boxed{} and comparing it to the ground truth answer under equivalence rules.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 step-by-step solution and 1 final boxed answer per problem
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Human evaluation participants were university students studying computer science; four were authors and two were friends or acquaintances of the authors.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Mathematica computer algebra system; Asymptote for figures/graphics; LaTeX for problem and solution formatting.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: No sensitive human attributes are collected as dataset fields. Human evaluation participants were university students; the paper mentions their academic background and that they were authors, friends, or acquaintances.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states the dataset is intended to better forecast reasoning capabilities and explicitly says it is not intended to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is drawn from competition mathematics problems and thus reflects high-school competition math, with subjects and difficulty levels chosen from that domain. The paper also notes that MATH is challenging for current models and that AMPS is curated and algorithmically generated.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: MATH is limited to competition mathematics problems and may not generalize beyond that domain. The paper notes that accuracy remains relatively low even for large models and that step-by-step solutions generated by models can be misleading or logically incorrect.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking, training, fine-tuning, testing, and validation of mathematical problem-solving models; pretraining on AMPS; evaluating exact-match answer generation and step-by-step solution generation. The paper says it should be used to better forecast reasoning capabilities, not to help students cheat on exams.
